claims.text: Incorporating detailed calculations of local lattice distortion and mass variance will more accurately identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity.
Chemical disorder enhances phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
The target materials are homogenized, single-phase, disordered high-entropy-alloy solid solutions with near-random elemental distributions and minimal secondary phases.
The proposed approach couples density-functional-theory vibrational calculations with statistical models of mass fluctuation and local lattice distortion.
Uniform microstructures and minimized contributions from grain boundaries and porosity are required for evaluating the approach.
Local lattice distortions and mass fluctuations caused by chemical disorder mediate increased phonon scattering.
Intrinsic chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys produces significant local lattice distortions.
Intrinsic chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys produces substantial mass variance.
Local lattice distortion and mass variance strengthen Rayleigh and disorder scattering of phonons.
Quantifying these scattering mechanisms refines estimates of phonon mean free path and lattice thermal conductivity.
The proposed model will be more accurate than conventional mixing-rule or Debye-based models.
The proposed method will predict lattice thermal conductivities approximately 25–50% lower than conventional mixing-rule estimates.
Experimental lattice thermal-conductivity measurements will agree with the proposed method's predictions within a 10% error margin.
Conventional mixing laws and standard Debye models do not adequately account for local lattice distortions caused by chemical disorder.
The approach is applicable only to homogeneously disordered, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The approach may be inaccurate for alloys with significant phase separation, ordering, or major microstructural defects.
The quantitative prediction of a 25–50% reduction is uncertain because synthesis and microstructural quality can vary.
